**Brite Payments launches pay-by-bank in the UK after FCA authorisation**

*The Swedish instant payments provider's UK entry adds another competitor to a market where pay-by-bank adoption is accelerating but reliability concerns persist.*

Brite Payments has begun offering pay-by-bank services in the UK after securing authorisation from the Financial Conduct Authority. Lena Hackeloer, the company's founder and chief executive, said the UK is one of the most mature open banking markets globally but that merchants still face gaps in the payment experience that Brite aims to address.

The move positions Brite alongside established providers such as TrueLayer, Yapily and Plaid in a UK market that crossed one billion open banking payments in July. Brite's model, built around instant settlement, is already live across several European markets and its UK entry signals continued confidence in account-to-account payments despite ongoing concerns about conversion rates and payment reliability that have dogged broader pay-by-bank adoption.

The UK's open banking payments market is becoming increasingly competitive. Recent months have seen Mollie acquire GoCardless, TrueLayer raise fresh capital with Italian state backing, and Nopan secure funding specifically to tackle payment reliability. Brite's arrival adds a well-capitalised Nordic player to a crowded field at a time when commercial variable recurring payments and the UK Payments Initiative are expanding the addressable market.

*Sources: [Brite Payments rolls out Pay by Bank in UK after securing FCA licence](https://www.abcmoney.co.uk/2026/10/brite-payments-rolls-out-pay-by-bank-in-uk-after-securing-fca-licence/) — ABC Money*

**Equifax integrates Mastercard Open Finance into its credit decisioning tools**

*The partnership gives lenders a second open finance provider alongside Equifax's existing credit file, extending the reach of consumer-permissioned cashflow data in US lending decisions.*

Equifax is integrating consumer-permissioned insights from Mastercard Open Finance into its open banking solutions, giving lenders and fintechs the option to source cashflow data through Mastercard's network alongside Equifax's own consumer credit file. The arrangement lets lenders choose their open finance provider rather than being locked into a single data source.

The tie-up reflects a broader trend in which credit bureaux are absorbing open banking data into their core products rather than treating it as a standalone offering. Experian launched a dedicated consumer reporting agency for cashflow-based underwriting earlier this month, and PayPoint completed its acquisition of AperiData in June to build open banking into credit data. Equifax's move to partner with Mastercard rather than build or acquire its own open finance capability signals a different strategic approach, one that leverages Mastercard's existing connectivity to bank accounts.

The integration is US-focused but has implications for European markets where Mastercard Open Finance operates. As FCA's open finance roadmap advances and the EU's financial data access regulation takes shape, traditional credit infrastructure on both sides of the Atlantic is having to accommodate permissioned account data, reshaping how lenders approach underwriting.

*Sources: [Equifax taps Mastercard Open Finance to give lenders more consumer-permissioned insights](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/111317/equifax-taps-mastercard-open-finance-to-give-lenders-more-consumer-permissioned-insights?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra | [Equifax (EFX), What Is Behind The Latest Attention?](https://simplywall.st/stocks/us/commercial-services/nyse-efx/equifax/news/equifax-efx-what-is-behind-the-latest-attention) — Simply Wall St News*

**Most SMEs see stablecoin potential for cross-border payments but few accept them**

*A stark gap exists between SME interest in stablecoins and actual adoption, with 88% of international SME finance professionals saying stablecoins could improve B2B collections yet only 27% currently accepting them.*

Research from Neo, a cross-border payments and treasury fintech, has found a stark gap between SME interest in stablecoins and actual adoption. Among senior finance professionals at internationally active SMEs, 88% said stablecoins could improve business-to-business (B2B) collections, but just 27% currently accept them for customer payments.

The findings arrive as stablecoin infrastructure in Europe matures rapidly. USDC became the EU's first significant e-money token designated under the Markets in Crypto-Assets regulation earlier this month, and several major banks have committed to a joint stablecoin venture with a euro-denominated token as an early priority. Mastercard integrated BVNK into its platform for unified fiat-stablecoin settlement, and Lloyds completed a live cross-border stablecoin payment with Visa in October.

While the rails are being built, practical barriers remain for smaller firms. Integration complexity, regulatory uncertainty across jurisdictions and limited counterparty readiness are likely factors. The survey points to a distribution and onboarding problem rather than a demand problem: stablecoins will not displace traditional correspondent banking for cross-border B2B flows until accepting them is as straightforward as accepting card or bank transfer payments.

*Sources: [Research reveals gaps in SME's stablecoin adoption](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/111312/research-reveals-gaps-in-smes-stablecoin-adoption?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*

**Japan's three largest banks complete joint stablecoin proof of concept**

*A coordinated test of jointly issued stablecoins for cross-border payments by Japan's banking establishment could influence how European banks approach collaborative digital money initiatives.*

Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corporation, Mizuho Bank and MUFG Bank, together with Mitsubishi UFJ Trust and Banking Corporation and TISI, completed a proof of concept for jointly issued stablecoins and cross-border payments between July 17 and July 23, 2024. The test explored how Japan's three largest banking groups could co-issue a stablecoin and use it for international settlement.

This model stands in contrast to the fragmented stablecoin strategies seen elsewhere. In Europe, a consortium of global banks announced plans for a joint stablecoin venture in September 2024 with a euro token as an early priority, but the initiative remains at an earlier stage. Japan's proof of concept demonstrates that the joint-issuance model can reach technical validation, even if commercial deployment is some way off.

The Japanese test also carries implications for the broader question of whether bank-issued stablecoins or central bank digital currencies will anchor future cross-border settlement. The ECB's digital euro is advancing through legislative negotiations, while Project Pontes aims to connect tokenised assets with central bank money. Japan's banks choosing to test a collaborative commercial model rather than wait for a CBDC suggests that at least some banking systems see private-sector stablecoins as the faster path to production use.

*Sources: [Japanese banks complete stablecoin PoC](https://www.finextra.com/pressarticle/111311/japanese-banks-complete-stablecoin-poc?utm_medium=rssfinextra&utm_source=finextrafeed) — Finextra*
